item.title: Macklem admits Bank of Canada offered mixed messaging on core inflation in past
item.description: The head of the Bank of Canada is admitting the central bank hasn’t always been clear in how it talks about its inflation target.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: The Bank of Canada is keeping firm to its two per cent inflation target, but it’s adjusting what it tracks to get there. The federal government and the Bank of Canada renewed the central bank’s five-year mandate earlier this month and maintained the target for two per cent annual inflation, as measured by Statistics Canada’s consumer price index, or CPI. The central bank maintains a one-to-three per cent band around that target, which offers some wiggle room to execute monetary policy. Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem spoke to a business crowd in Toronto on Tuesday where he hailed the two per cent target as a “clear and well-understood objective” since it was implemented in 1995. Anchoring its policy rate decisions on that inflation target helped the Bank of Canada tame the post-COVID surge in inflation, Macklem argued in prepared remarks. But he acknowledged that Canadians didn’t respond well to inflation and the rate hikes it necessitated. “For many Canadians, it was their first experience with high inflation. And they didn’t like it. As we reviewed our framework, we held consultations across the country to hear from Canadians. We heard a lot of anger,” Macklem said. The head of the Bank of Canada acknowledged in his speech that the central bank could have done a better job in the post-pandemic period, which saw inflation pressures compound after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Monetary policymakers were “too slow to recognize the persistence of inflationary pressures and how broadly they were spreading through the economy,” Macklem said. He also acknowledged that the Bank of Canada has, at times, put focus on different measures of core inflation to track underlying price trends. The Bank of Canada previously downplayed its preferred measures of core inflation, CPI-trim and CPI-median, as it tried to gauge how supply shocks were affecting the economy. “We wanted to be transparent about where we saw inflation pressures and where we did not. But we weren’t as clear as we hoped,” Macklem said. “Canadians found it confusing when we discussed measures that strip out volatile prices such as food and gasoline. After all, these are important parts of the family budget. And financial market participants sometimes felt that we were moving the inflation goalposts.” Excluding the right measures can help give the Bank of Canada a clearer picture of inflation trends and cut through temporary forces pushing prices higher, Macklem said. Now, the Bank of Canada will put its focus back on an old measure called CPIX, which excludes eight fixed sets of items from the inflation calculation to provide a consistent benchmark of how prices are evolving. The Bank of Canada used CPIX to guide monetary policy decisions from 2001 to 2016. Some of the items excluded from CPIX are gasoline, mortgage interest costs and fruits and vegetables. The central bank will retain what’s called CPI-trim as its other core measure, which strips out the items seeing the most extreme price changes in each month. Macklem explained that, while the Bank of Canada’s updated core metrics can help monetary policymakers see where prices are headed, keeping overall inflation at two per cent remains the central bank’s north star. “Total CPI inflation is our target, and it will be front and centre in all our communications. Various indicators help us understand where inflation is headed and the risks around that forecast. But they are inputs to our analysis, not targets,” he said. -- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

item.title: World stocks are mixed after Wall Street's rebound as Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia’s CEO
item.description: HONG KONG — Global stocks were mixed Tuesday after a rally on Wall Street as Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia’s CEO. U.S. futures edged higher. Oil prices extended their losses, falling close to their ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry are leading the U.S. market lower once again on Tuesday. That’s even though much of the rest of Wall Street is rising, along with confidence among Americans in the economy. The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent after dropping as much as 1.4 per cent earlier, and it’s heading toward its eighth loss in the last nine days. Tech stocks led the way lower in a turnaround from Monday’s surge and dragged the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 1.3 per cent, as of 10:05 a.m. Eastern time. But the majority of U.S. stocks were nevertheless rising, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 271 points, or 0.5 per cent. It’s the latest swing for a market that has been mostly sinking since setting its all-time high last month. The worry is that prices for AI-related stocks shot too high into a possible bubble and need to deflate. That carries immense consequences for the broader market and workers’ 401(k) accounts because AI stocks have grown so big that they’ve become Wall Street’s most influential sector. While the return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang does bring back a charismatic leader who championed and helped build the entire AI industry, it does not settle the deep concerns dogging it. For one, doubts remain about whether AI can possibly produce enough profit and productivity to make the massive investments underway in data centres worth it. At the same time, high interest rates in the bond market caused in part by the war with Iran are making it more difficult to borrow money to pay for the industry’s growth. Sweeping victories for Democrats earlier this month in the U.S. midterm elections, meanwhile, have raised concerns about more regulation for AI, including possible halts to further construction of data centres. To be sure, AI stocks and the broader U.S. market have been prone to extreme reversals since the summer, not only week to week but even hour to hour. For now, at least, the momentum is back downward. Nvidia fell 6.6 per cent a day after soaring 31.5 per cent to its biggest gain in more than two decades. Other stocks around the AI industry fell by similar amounts. CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and rents out access to them over the cloud, sank 9 per cent. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centres, fell 4.6 per cent. And Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, tumbled 7.4 per cent to drop below US$83. That’s how much Anthropic first sold its stock for in its initial public offering last week. The stock had briefly jumped as high as US$115 in its first day of trading amid a frenzy of hype. Such drops were powerful enough to offset gains for the slight majority of stocks on Wall Street. They rose following the latest report to say confidence among U.S. consumers is improving by more than economists expected. Companies in industries across the economy also continue to report strong growth in profits for the summer. That helped the majority of stocks within the S&P 500 to rise. Dollar Tree climbed 11.3 per cent after reporting better earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The average shopper spent slightly more in its stores during the three months than a year earlier, and more of them came than last year. Kohl’s rallied 13 per cent after reporting a profit for the latest quarter, when analysts were expecting basically zero. It also gave forecasts for revenue for the final three months of its fiscal year that were better than expected. The retailers are among the latest companies to join the long list of big U.S. companies delivering bigger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Businesses in the S&P 500 are on pace to report overall growth in earnings per share of more than 25 per cent for a third straight quarter, according to FactSet. Stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits and interest rates over the long term. But emotions of investors can also overwhelm them in the short term, as the last few weeks have demonstrated. In the bond market, Treasury yields slipped as investors moved into investments seen as safer bets. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.91 per cent from 4.92 per cent late Monday. That was despite a rise in oil prices, which tend to push upward on inflation and on bond yields. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 1.8 per cent to US$88.26. It’s been yo-yoing between US$72 and US$114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 6.3 per cent, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 rallied 3.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves, as they caught up to Monday’s surge from Wall Street. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Writer Elaine Lai contributed to this report

item.title: Oil and gas drillers optimistic heading into 2027, but warn of labour shortages
item.description: Oil and gas service firms say improving market conditions and a more supportive political climate are expected to bolster Canadian drilling activity next year.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: CALGARY — Oil and gas service firms say improving market conditions and a more supportive political climate are expected to bolster Canadian drilling activity next year, but labour shortfalls could threaten that momentum. Industry advocacy group Enserva has released its annual state of the industry report, which calls for an increase in the number of wells drilled in 2027 versus this year. But it flags competition for workers as a major challenge at a time when artificial intelligence data centres and major infrastructure projects draw from the same talent pool. Bradley Fedora, president and CEO of Trican Well Service Ltd., says the prospect of “hyperinflation” in the cost of labour and materials is what scares him most. Thomas Alford, president of completion and production services at Precision Drilling, told reporters at the event that it can take up to eight years to train up a competent drill rig staffer, and the industry has been so unstable in recent years that it’s been hard for those workers to get that consistent job experience. Gurpreet Lail, Enserva’s president and CEO, says the sector needs to work hard to attract and keep talent as data centre developments offer big paycheques to tradespeople and perks that have until now been “unheard of.” --- Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.
